paragraphs: Even before the war, however, the balance between the old civilizations and the new resources was in danger. Europe's wealth depended on two facts. First, America had a large surplus of food to export. So Europe could buy food cheaply, measured by the labour needed to make its own exports. Second, because of its earlier investments abroad, Europe received a large amount of money every year without paying anything in return. The second fact then seemed safe. But the first was less secure, because the population overseas was growing, mainly in the United States.

When the new soils of America first started to produce crops, the population there was very small compared with Europe. So their own local needs were small too. As late as 1890, Europe had three times as many people as North and South America together. But by 1914, the United States needed almost all the wheat it produced. It was clearly close to the time when it would have wheat to export only in years with an unusually good harvest. In fact, the present needs of the United States are thought to be more than ninety per cent of the average harvest of the five years from 1909 to 1913. At that time, however, the growing pressure did not appear as a shortage. It appeared as a steady rise in real cost. In other words, there was no lack of wheat in the world as a whole. But to get enough of it, buyers had to offer a higher real price. The best thing in the situation was that Central and Western Europe was largely fed by the export surplus of Russia and Roumania.

In short, Europe's claim on the resources of the New World was becoming uncertain. The law of diminishing returns was coming back into force. Each year, Europe had to offer more of its other goods to get the same amount of bread. For this reason, Europe could not afford trouble in any of its main sources of supply.

Much more could be said about the special economic features of Europe in 1914. I have chosen to stress the three or four greatest causes of instability. The first was a very large population that depended for its living on a complex and artificial system. The second was the unsettled state of mind of the working and capitalist classes. The third was Europe's uncertain claim on the food of the New World, together with its complete dependence on it.

The war shook this system so badly that it put the whole life of Europe in danger. A great part of the Continent was sick and dying. Its population was far larger than the number of people who could find a living. Its organization was destroyed, its transport system was broken, and its food supplies were terribly damaged.
